name: Bexarotene

lead: Bexarotene (Targretin) is a prescription retinoid taken as a capsule or applied as a gel. It is approved for the skin lesions of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
In trials, about half of people with early-stage disease responded, with plaques becoming flatter and clearer.

paras: It activates retinoid X receptors, which partner with other nuclear receptors to regulate cell growth and differentiation.
Common effects are high triglycerides and cholesterol, central hypothyroidism and headache. The label has a boxed warning for birth defects. It is Rx-only.

chain: Regulates skin cell growth and differentiation
Lymphoma skin plaques flatten or clear
angle.text: Bexarotene is prescribed to improve skin lesions of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Trials reported reduced plaque elevation, and a small psoriasis study found improved severity with oral use.

lead: Bexarotene (Targretin) is an oral and topical retinoid that selectively activates retinoid X receptors (RXRs). It is FDA-approved for the skin manifestations of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, where it is used to improve skin lesions.[1][2]

In appearance communities it is discussed as a retinoid-class compound, but its documented use is medical: treatment of refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, including mycosis fungoides.[3] Clearing or flattening skin plaques is the visible result in that setting.[2]
The US label carries a boxed warning for birth defects, and common effects include raised blood lipids and central hypothyroidism.[1][2]
infobox: Rx-only; boxed warning for birth defects

paras: The oral capsule is indicated for cutaneous manifestations of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients refractory to at least one prior systemic therapy.[1] A topical gel was cleared in 2000 for early-stage CTCL skin lesions.[4] Mycosis fungoides, the most common CTCL subtype, may be treated with oral bexarotene after skin-directed therapies.[3] Bexarotene has also been a comparator in the ALCANZA trial.[5]

In refractory or persistent early-stage CTCL, the overall response rate was 54% with oral bexarotene; in advanced-stage disease it was 45%.[2] Topical bexarotene produced response rates of 44% to 63% in early-stage CTCL in separate trials.[2] A multinational phase II-III trial in refractory advanced CTCL enrolled 94 patients.[6] In psoriasis, oral bexarotene reduced plaque elevation and severity in a trial summarized in a review.[2] In ALCANZA, bexarotene or methotrexate was the physician's-choice arm against brentuximab vedotin.[5]

The most common adverse events with oral bexarotene are elevated triglycerides and cholesterol, central hypothyroidism and headache; reversible pancreatitis has been reported.[2] The drug suppresses TSH and free thyroxine, and is listed among causes of drug-induced central hypothyroidism.[7] The label lists hyperlipidemia, pancreatitis, liver toxicity, hypothyroidism, neutropenia and cataracts as warnings, and contraindicates pregnancy because of birth defects.[1]

Bexarotene binds RXR alpha, beta and gamma, which pair with partners including retinoic acid receptors, the vitamin D receptor, thyroid receptor and PPARs to regulate gene expression for differentiation and proliferation.[1][2]
Bexarotene (LGD-1069) from Ligand was the first RXR-selective retinoid to enter clinical trials; Targretin capsules launched in the US in January 2000 for CTCL.[4]
Bexarotene has been studied in lung, breast and other cancers, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease models.[8][9][10]

timeline.event: FDA approves Targretin capsules for CTCL.[4]
